agree.reason: Opening with Dana's own $600K quote and a specific before-and-after result could earn a reply, but the email never shows the savings next to the cost, and it never tells the IT director how little his team would have to do.

honest.reason: It wisely leaves out the claim that errors were "cut in half" across customers and gives only the one customer's numbers, but it presents that best case without saying it's the best one, and it ends by suggesting her numbers could move "the same way" when the only other reported result was 2.8 to 2.2.

works_the_facts.reason: It derives nothing from the figures: no 54% reduction, no estimate that the same drop would save roughly $320K of her $600K, and no comparison with about $75K a year for five sites.

right_comparison.reason: It names the $600K a year she loses now, but it never sets that ongoing loss against the price or the likely savings, so doing nothing never looks like the costlier choice.

qualification.reason: Results ranged from a 54% drop to a 21% drop, so a hedge was needed, but the only one is the vague "whether your numbers could move the same way", with no range, no checkpoint and no consequence if the target is missed.

objections.reason: "Doesn't replace your WMS, sits on top of it" and the three-week setup partly answer the IT director's resistance, but the email doesn't say what IT would actually have to do or whether the existing system is touched at all.

fit.reason: It is short, the paragraphs are easy to read on a phone and it ends with a clear request for a call, as the brief asked.
